claim: The WASH complex is composed of five core protein components: WASHC1 (aka WASH1), WASHC2 (aka FAM21), WASHC3 (aka CCDC53), WASHC4 (aka SWIP), and WASHC5 (aka Strumpellin).
source: WASH is composed of five core protein components: WASHC1 (aka WASH1), WASHC2 (aka FAM21), WASHC3 (aka CCDC53), WASHC4 (aka SWIP), and WASHC5 (aka Strumpellin) (encoded by genes Washc1-Washc5, respectively), which are broadly expressed in multiple organ systems (Alekhina et al., 2017; Kustermann et al., 2018; McNally et al., 2017; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Thul et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with supporting citations.

claim: WASH complex proteins are broadly expressed in multiple organ systems.
source: WASH is composed of five core protein components: WASHC1 (aka WASH1), WASHC2 (aka FAM21), WASHC3 (aka CCDC53), WASHC4 (aka SWIP), and WASHC5 (aka Strumpellin) (encoded by genes Washc1-Washc5, respectively), which are broadly expressed in multiple organ systems (Alekhina et al., 2017; Kustermann et al., 2018; McNally et al., 2017; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Thul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The WASH complex plays a central role in non-neuronal endosomal trafficking by activating Arp2/3-dependent actin branching at the outer surface of endosomes.
source: The WASH complex plays a central role in non-neuronal endosomal trafficking by activating Arp2/3-dependent actin branching at the outer surface of endosomes to influence cargo sorting and vesicular scission (Gomez and Billadeau, 2009; Lee et al., 2016; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Piotrowski et al., 2013; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations from prior research.

claim: WASH interacts with at least three main cargo adaptor complexes: the Retromer, Retriever, and COMMD/CCDC22/CCDC93 (CCC) complexes.
source: WASH also interacts with at least three main cargo adaptor complexes – the Retromer, Retriever, and COMMD/CCDC22/CCDC93 (CCC) complexes – all of which associate with distinct sorting nexins to select specific cargo and enable their trafficking to other cellular locations (Binda et al., 2019; Farfán et al., 2013; McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Seaman and Freeman, 2014; Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with supporting citations.

claim: Loss of the WASH complex in non-neuronal cells results in aberrant endosomal tubule elongation and cargo mislocalization.
source: Loss of the WASH complex in non-neuronal cells has detrimental effects on endosomal structure and function, as its loss results in aberrant endosomal tubule elongation and cargo mislocalization (Bartuzi et al., 2016; Derivery et al., 2009; Gomez et al., 2012; Gomez and Billadeau, 2009; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Piotrowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations from prior research.

claim: Dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (protein: Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8).
source: Consistent with the association between the endosomal trafficking system and pathology, dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (protein: Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8) (de Bot et al., 2013; Valdmanis et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (protein: SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities.
source: Consistent with the association between the endosomal trafficking system and pathology, dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (protein: Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8) (de Bot et al., 2013; Valdmanis et al., 2007), and autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (protein: SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities (Assoum et al., 2020; Elliott et al., 2013; Ropers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: An autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) was identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability.
source: In particular, an autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) was identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability (Ropers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: Cell lines derived from SWIPP1019R patients exhibited decreased abundance of WASH proteins.
source: Cell lines derived from these patients exhibited decreased abundance of WASH proteins, leading the authors to hypothesize that the observed cognitive deficits in SWIPP1019R patients resulted from disruption of neuronal WASH signaling (Ropers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome identified by iBioID includes 175 proteins that were significantly enriched.
source: The resulting neuronal WASH proteome included 175 proteins that were significantly enriched (fold-change≥4.0, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05, Figure 1G; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to data analysis methods and a figure.

claim: All five WASH complex components were identified in the neuronal WASH proteome.
source: Of these proteins, we identified all five WASH complex components (Figure 1H), as well as 13 previously reported WASH complex interactors (Figure 1I; McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Singla et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1H showing the data.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome includes 13 previously reported WASH complex interactors.
source: Of these proteins, we identified all five WASH complex components (Figure 1H), as well as 13 previously reported WASH complex interactors (Figure 1I; McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Singla et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1I and supporting citations.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome includes 23 proteins enriched for endosomal functions.
source: Additional bioinformatic analyses of the neuronal WASH proteome identified a network of proteins implicated in vesicular trafficking, including 23 proteins enriched for endosomal functions (Figure 1J) and 24 proteins enriched for endocytic functions (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1J.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome includes 24 proteins enriched for endocytic functions.
source: Additional bioinformatic analyses of the neuronal WASH proteome identified a network of proteins implicated in vesicular trafficking, including 23 proteins enriched for endosomal functions (Figure 1J) and 24 proteins enriched for endocytic functions (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1K.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome includes 31 proteins enriched for cytoskeletal regulatory functions.
source: Furthermore, there were 31 proteins enriched for cytoskeletal regulatory functions (Figure 1L), including actin-modulatory molecules such as the Arp2/3 complex subunit ARPC5
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1L.

claim: The neuronal WASH proteome includes 27 proteins known to localize to the excitatory post-synapse.
source: The WASH1-BioID2 isolated complex also contained 27 proteins known to localize to the excitatory post-synapse (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: A mouse model of the human WASHC4c.3056C>G mutation was generated using CRISPR.
source: To determine how disruption of the WASH complex may lead to disease, we generated a mouse model of a human missense mutation found in children with intellectual disability, WASHC4c.3056c>g (protein: SWIPP1019R) (Ropers et al., 2011). Due to the sequence homology of human and mouse Washc4 genes, we were able to introduce the same point mutation in exon 29 of murine Washc4 using CRISPR (Derivery and Gautreau, 2010; Ropers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Homozygous SWIPP1019R mutant mice display significantly decreased abundance of Strumpellin and WASH1 in brain lysate.
source: Western blot analysis of brain lysate from adult homozygous SWIPP1019R mutant mice (referred to from here on as MUT mice) displayed significantly decreased abundance of two WASH complex members, Strumpellin and WASH1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 2B showing the data.

claim: SWIPP1019R mutation results in decreased co-immunoprecipitation with Strumpellin and WASH1 compared to wild-type SWIP.
source: To test whether this mutation disrupted interactions between WASH complex subunits, we compared the ability of wild-type SWIP (WT) and SWIPP1019R (MUT) to co-immunoprecipitate with Strumpellin and WASH1 in HEK cells. Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively), suggesting that the SWIPP1019R mutation hinders WASH complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing the data.

claim: Spatial proteomics analysis of SWIPP1019R mouse brain identified 6919 reproducibly quantified proteins.
source: By performing this experiment in triplicate, deep coverage of the mouse brain proteome was obtained – across all 48 samples we quantified 86,551 peptides, corresponding to 7488 proteins. After data pre-processing, normalization, and filtering, we retained 6919 reproducibly quantified proteins in the final dataset (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the dataset.

claim: 65 proteins had significantly altered abundance in at least one of the seven subcellular fractions between WT and MUT brain.
source: In the first analysis, there were 65 proteins with significantly altered abundance in at least one of the seven subcellular fractions (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the supplementary data file.

claim: Five proteins were differentially abundant between WT and MUT in all seven fractions, including four WASH proteins and RAB21A.
source: Five proteins were differentially abundant between WT and MUT in all seven fractions, including four WASH proteins (WASHC1, WASHC2, WASHC4, WASHC5) and RAB21A – a known WASH interactor that functions in early endosomal trafficking ( Figure 3D; Del Olmo et al., 2019; Simpson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 3D and supporting citations.

claim: 728 proteins were differentially abundant between WT and MUT brain across all fractions.
source: Next, to evaluate global differences between WT and MUT brain, we analyzed the average effect of genotype on protein abundance across all fractions using MSstatsTMT (Huang et al., 2020). At this level, there were 728 differentially abundant proteins between WT and MUT brain (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the analysis method and supplementary data.

claim: Clustering of the protein covariation graph identified 49 modules of proteins that strongly covaried together.
source: Clustering of the protein covariation graph identified 49 modules of proteins that strongly covaried together (see Materials and methods for complete description of clustering approach).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the methods section.

claim: 23 of the 49 modules exhibited significant differences in WT versus MUT brain.
source: Twenty-three of the 49 modules exhibited significant differences in WT versus MUT brain (Bonferroni p-adjust < 0.05; Supplementary file 3; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Hochberg, 1988).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the statistical analysis and supplementary data.

claim: Module 38 (M38) contains the WASH complex and was predicted to have endosomal function.
source: Of note, the module containing the WASH complex, M38, was predicted to have endosomal function by annotation of protein function (UniProt: 'Early Endosome', hypergeometric test p-adjust < 0.05, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to the statistical analysis and supplementary data.

claim: M38 contains components of the CCC and Retriever sorting complexes.
source: Similar to the WASH iBioID proteome (Figure 1), M38 contained many endosomal proteins, including components of the CCC (CCDC22, CCDC93, COMMD1-3, and COMMD6-7) and Retriever sorting complexes (VPS26C and VPS35L) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: M38 contains core subunits of the CORVET and HOPS vesicular tethering complexes.
source: It also contained core subunits of the CORVET and HOPS vesicular tethering complexes, which enable fusion of vesicles within the endo-lysosomal system (VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, and VPS33A) (van der Beek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: The abundance of M38 was significantly lower in MUT brain compared to WT.
source: Across all fractions, the abundance of M38 was significantly lower in MUT brain compared to WT, providing evidence that the SWIPP1019R mutation reduces the stability of this protein subnetwork and impairs its function (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 3C showing the data.

claim: Module 36 (M36) was enriched for lysosomal protein components and exhibited increased abundance in MUT brain.
source: We also observed another module, M36, that was enriched for lysosomal protein components (hypergeometric test p-adjust <0.05) (Geladaki et al., 2019) and contained all eight subunits of the exocyst complex (CORUM), a vesicular trafficking complex involved in lysosomal secretion (Giurgiu et al., 2019; Sáez et al., 2019). In contrast to the decreased abundance of the WASH complex/endosome module (M38), M36 exhibited increased abundance in MUT brain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 4C and supporting citations.

claim: M36 contains several lysosomal cathepsin proteases and key lysosomal hydrolases.
source: M36 (Figure 4B) contained several lysosomal cathepsin proteases (CTSA, CTSB, CTSS, and CTSL) as well as key lysosomal hydrolases (HEXA, GBA, GLB1, MAN2B1, and MAN2B2) (Eng and Desnick, 1994; Mayor et al., 1993; Mok et al., 2003; Moon et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2018; Regier and Tifft, 1993; Rosenbaum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 4B and supporting citations.

claim: M36 contains the lysosomal glycoprotein progranulin (GRN).
source: Notably, M36 also contained the lysosomal glycoprotein progranulin (GRN), which is integral to proper lysosome function and whose loss is widely linked with neurodegenerative pathologies (Baker et al., 2006; Pottier et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: MUT neurons display larger EEA1+ somatic puncta than WT neurons.
source: Reconstructed three-dimensional volumes of EEA1 and Cathepsin D puncta revealed that MUT neurons display larger EEA1+ somatic puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5G and J), but no difference in the total number of EEA1+ puncta (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 5G and J showing the data.

claim: MUT neurons exhibit significantly less Cathepsin D+ puncta than WT neurons.
source: Conversely, MUT neurons exhibited significantly less Cathepsin D+ puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5H), but the remaining puncta were significantly larger than those of WT neurons (Figure 5I and K).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 5H, I, and K showing the data.

claim: MUT motor cortices display significantly greater cleaved caspase-3 staining compared to age-matched WT littermate controls at 10 months old.
source: However, at 10mo, the MUT motor cortices displayed significantly greater cleaved caspsase-3 staining compared to age-matched WT littermate controls (Figures 6D, E and H).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 6D, E, and H showing the data.

claim: Large electron-dense inclusions were observed in the cell bodies of MUT neurons.
source: Strikingly, we observed large electron-dense inclusions in the cell bodies of MUT neurons (arrows, Figure 6L; pseudo-colored region, 6N).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 6L and 6N showing the data.

claim: The electron-dense structures in MUT neurons were associated with electron-lucent lipid-like inclusions, supporting the conclusion that these structures were lipofuscin accumulation at lysosomal residual bodies.
source: These dense structures were associated electron-lucent lipid-like inclusions (asterisk, Figure 6N), which supported the conclusion that these structures were lipofuscin accumulation at lysosomal residual bodies (Poët et al., 2006; Valdez et al., 2017; Yoshikawa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 6N and supporting citations.

claim: MUT mice showed a significant decrease in conditioned freezing to tone presentation compared to WT littermates 48 hours after fear conditioning.
source: Forty-eight hours after exposure to the paired tone and footshock, MUT mice showed a significant decrease in conditioned freezing to tone presentation compared to their WT littermates (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 7B and C showing the data.

claim: The deficit in fear response was evident at both adolescence and adulthood.
source: Additionally, this deficit in fear response was evident at both adolescence and adulthood (top panels, and bottom panels, respectively, Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 7B and C showing the data.

claim: MUT mice performed markedly worse than WT littermate controls on the rotarod at both adolescence and adulthood.
source: At both adolescence and adulthood, MUT mice performed markedly worse than WT littermate controls (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 8C showing the data.

claim: At adulthood, MUT mice display significantly longer rear swing time compared to WT mice.
source: At 5.5mo (bottom), MUT mice display significantly longer rear swing time (WT 140 ± 6.2 ms, MUT 252.0 ± 21.6 ms, t12=4.988, p=0.0003).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 8E showing the data and statistical analysis.

claim: At adulthood, MUT mice take significantly longer strides with their hindlimbs compared to WT mice.
source: At 5.5mo (bottom), MUT mice take significantly longer strides with their hindlimbs (WT 60.8 ± 0.8 mm, MUT 73.6 ± 2.7 mm, t11.7=4.547, p=0.0007).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 8F showing the data and statistical analysis.

claim: At adulthood, MUT mice display decreased homologous coupling, suggestive of abnormal gait symmetry.
source: At 5.5 mo (bottom), MUT mice display decreased homologous coupling, suggestive of abnormal gait symmetry (WT 0.48 ± 0.003, MUT 0.46 ± 0.004, t18.8=3.715, p=0.0015).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 8G showing the data and statistical analysis.

claim: All human SWIPP1019R patients exhibited motor symptoms including fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria.
source: While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms (mean age=10.4 years old, Figure 8H). The patients' movements were described as 'clumsy' with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 8H showing the clinical data.

claim: SWIPP1019R causes a loss of WASH complex function, resulting in endo-lysosomal disruption.
source: Taken together, the data presented here support a mechanistic model whereby SWIPP1019R causes a loss of WASH complex function, resulting in endo-lysosomal disruption and accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, such as upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, as well as build-up of lipofuscin and cleaved caspase-3 over time.
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a summary of the findings.

claim: Loss of WASH complex function leads to cognitive deficits and progressive motor impairments.
source: To our knowledge, this study provides the first mechanistic evidence of WASH complex impairment having direct and indirect organellar effects that lead to cognitive deficits and progressive motor impairments (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a summary of the findings with reference to Figure 9.

claim: The neuronal WASH complex closely interacts with the CCC and Retriever cargo selective complexes.
source: Using in vivo proximity-based proteomics in wild-type mouse brain, we found that the WASH complex closely interacts with the CCC (COMMD9 and CCDC93) and Retriever (VPS35L) cargo selective complexes (Bartuzi et al., 2016; Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Loss of WASH function may lead to increased accumulation of cargo at early endosomes.
source: We speculate that loss of WASH function in our mutant mouse model may lead to increased accumulation of cargo and associated machinery at early endosomes (as seen in Figure 5, enlarged EEA1+ puncta), eventually overburdening early endosomal vesicles and triggering transition to late endosomes for subsequent fusion with degradative lysosomes (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated explicitly as speculation based on the data, with reference to Figures 5 and 9.

claim: Elevated ER stress modulators can be indicative of neurodegenerative states.
source: This elevation of ER stress modulators can be indicative of neurodegenerative states, in which the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated to resolve misfolded species (Garcia-Huerta et al., 2016; Hetz and Saxena, 2017).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in mediators of the endo-lysosomal system are implicated in neurological diseases such as Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs), and hereditary spastic paraplegia.
source: It has become clear that preservation of the endo-lysosomal system is critical to neuronal function, as mutations in mediators of this process are implicated in neurological diseases such as Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs), and hereditary spastic paraplegia (Baker et al., 2006; Connor-Robson et al., 2019; Edvardson et al., 2012; Follett et al., 2019; Harold et al., 2009; Mukherjee et al., 2019; Pal et al., 2006; International Parkinsonism Genetics Network et al., 2013; Seshadri et al., 2010; Tachibana et al., 2019; Valdmanis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in the retromer protein VPS35 are associated with Parkinson's disease.
source: In particular, mutations associated with Parkinson's disease have been found in a close endosomal interactor of the WASH complex – the retromer protein VPS35 (VPS35D620N and VPS35R524W) – and have been linked to pathological α-synuclein aggregation in vitro (Chen et al., 2019; Follett et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: The SWIPP1019R mouse model does not display dopaminergic cell-specific changes.
source: In addition, unlike many Parkinson's disease models, which display specific deficits in dopaminergic cells, we did not observe any dopaminergic cell-specific changes in SWIPP1019R brain (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing the data.

claim: The SWIPP1019R model exhibits parallels to NCL models.
source: While our SWIPP1019R model appears to diverge in pathology from Parkinson's disease models, it does exhibit parallels to NCL models.
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a comparison.

claim: NCLs are lysosomal storage disorders primarily found in children.
source: NCLs are lysosomal storage disorders primarily found in children rather than adults, with heterogenous presentations and multigenic causations (Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: Most NCL patients present with marked neurological impairments and have the unifying feature of lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation.
source: Most patients present with marked neurological impairments, such as learning disabilities, motor abnormalities, vision loss, and seizures, and have the unifying feature of lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation upon pathological examination (Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: Loss of WASH complex function leads to phenotypes bearing strong resemblance to NCLs, including lipofuscin accumulation.
source: While the human SWIPP1019R mutation has not been classified as an NCL (Ropers et al., 2011), findings from our mutant mouse model suggest that loss of WASH complex function leads to phenotypes bearing strong resemblance to NCLs, including lipofuscin accumulation (Figures 5–8).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with reference to Figures 5-8 showing the data and a supporting citation.
